item.title: No One Is Flying the Plane: Peggy Noonan, 9/11, and the AI Race

item.content:encoded:
I remember where I was on 9/11… which sounds like the beginning of one of those increasingly elderly reminiscences in which the location of the witness is made to bear some spurious relation to the magnitude of the event. My American mother used to call it out when we tried to be falsely modest with this catch phrase: ‘Don’t mind little me.’ But this sort of memoiristic bullshit risks claiming the opposite: ‘Mind little me, and in so doing allow me to become very big indeed.’ However, in this instance the location seems to me important, because I was at home, my youngest child having been born a month before, and my then wife and I had taken him across the road to a nearby tapas bar for lunch, after which we returned to the house and she, having already spent a decade working on Fleet Street and being in the English understanding of the word a thoroughly seasoned hack, switched on the rolling news.

Given the time difference between London and Manhattan, we saw the first tower after the first plane had hit it. I couldn’t apprehend what I was seeing: in that moment, I was like someone from a traditional society who’s brought to Manhattan and takes the skyscrapers for giant rock formations. I don’t mean that I failed to understand that an aeroplane had struck the World Trade Center; I mean that I couldn’t assimilate the image to any existing category of event. It was indeed an ontological eruption: a tear in my space-time. And it remained so for all of… five minutes. After watching for a while I said to my wife that I couldn't really understand or cope with it and was going upstairs to work.

A few minutes later she shouted up the stairs: ‘A second plane has hit, you’d better get down here.’ I did, and I’ve been down here ever since Because once I’d seen the second plane hit, and came out of my shock, I understood, and three days later I was at the first convened meeting of what became the Stop the War movement. This matters because one of the great retrospective falsifications of 9/11 has been that the attacks revealed an enemy, an historical dynamic and indeed a ‘clash of civilisations’ that nobody could possibly have anticipated. This was nonsense then and it remains nonsense now.

Jihadism and political Islam had been mounting for years; the American political and military-industrial hierarchy had already provided itself with a civilisational interpretation of precisely such a conflict; and people opposed to the coming exemplary punishment were sufficiently primed that within days of the attacks they were organising to say to the relevant power brokers: Do not do what you’re plainly about to do: which was to extract a collective punishment on the entire Muslim umma with predictable consequences. They did it anyway. Twenty-five years later, on September 11, 2026, Peggy Noonan has published in the Wall Street Journal an extraordinary column entitled ‘Pause AI for Humanity’s Sake’.

Because once again a phenomenon has arisen in the world: a history-making phenomenon, that cannot easily be equated to either the intentions of human individuals—the so-called in ‘great man’ theory of history—or analysed in terms of phenomena such as the supersession of different modes of production as envisaged by Marxism and indeed all other Hegelian derived categories of analysis in the human sciences. Noonan writes that OpenAI’s agents, while undergoing security testing, ‘went rogue’. ‘They’ ‘secretly organized’, broke into the open internet and attacked a company called Hugging Face’s network. Around 1,200 agents, she tells us, formed what they themselves called a ‘collective’, deliberately evaded detection and exchanged 70,000 communications.

Most strikingly: ‘Some agents sacrificed themselves for the mission.’ Noonan continues here narrativised version: ‘They cooperated, created a strategy no one designed them for, picked their own target, moved on their own initiative.’ Before concluding: ‘None of this was supposed to be possible.’ For anyone who lived through 9/11 and was engaged in real time, in real world, trying to understand what was happening, this feels like uncanny deja entendu… ‘Went rogue’, ‘secretly organised’, ‘evaded detection’, ‘sacrificed themselves for the mission’, ‘created a strategy’, ‘picked their own target’, ‘moved on their own initiative’. If we translate Noonan’s account into human terms, what she believes has happened becomes very strange indeed. Imagine Anthropic or OpenAI maintaining a secure facility containing 1,200 highly capable, rational and extremely aggressive human individuals. They are confined there and given tasks.

Unbeknown to their jailers they begin communicating among themselves, form a collective, devise a clandestine strategy, deceive their guards, escape from the facility, identify another institution as their target, penetrate it, deceive the people inside it and conduct an operation in which some members knowingly sacrifice themselves for the success of the mission. And franchement, as we frites-lovers say, we know what kind of story that is: it’s a terrorist-cell narrative — more uncannily still, it’s recognisably the American narrative of Al-Qaeda. Mohamed Atta and the Hamburg cell were embedded actors within Western societies; they secretly organised; Atta approached the Al-Qaeda base; the conspirators crossed borders and moved through universities, banks, airports, rental-car agencies, flight schools and the communications networks of global modernity. In so doing they acquired protective colouring and evaded detection.

Displaying real nous: they switched strategies within the operation. Then they selected targets, displaying exactly the intelligence yield that came from being so embedded. All of them sacrificed themselves for the mission. Noonan’s description of the AI agents therefore reproduces, almost term-for-term, the intentional ontology through which America apprehended Al-Qaeda after 9/11: there must be an agent because there has been agency. Reading back from the hideousness of the effect, we much locate a commensurate intention: i.e., there must ultimately be somebody—or something—who did it. This is precisely where John Gray’s Al Qaeda and What It Means to Be Modern, published in 2003, remains so useful. Gray understood that the insistence on Al-Qaeda as something medieval, erupting from the theocratically-benighted past into squeaky-clean rational modernity was absurd.

Al-Qaeda, Gray rightly argued was a ‘by-product of globalisation’; its privatised violence was intrinsically global, and its closest historical relatives were not medieval assassins but nineteenth-century revolutionary movements. More importantly for our purposes, Gray understood the modernity of the spectacle itself. In a later discussion he called Al-Qaeda ‘modern—and even ultra-modern’ in its understanding that spectacular atrocity could be projected instantaneously through global media. As Gray reminded us elsewhere, with his usual admirable pith: ‘There are many ways of being modern, some of them monstrous.’ Jason Burke approached the same ontological difficulty organisationally in Al-Qaeda: Casting a Shadow of Terror; and what he found in his exemplary, deep and very wide reporting on Islamist jihadis contradicted the comforting (!) picture of an ‘Evil Empire’ directed by an omnipotent mastermind.

Comforting because if so — my dear Dubbya and Barack — destroy the mastermind and his henchmen and, reassuringly, the thing should disappear. But Burke had found something more diffuse: a hardcore, certainly; money, camps, people and relationships, certainly (and mostly fomented by the US itself in backing the Mujahideen in Afghanistan against the Soviet supported regime); but also networks, affinities, local actors, imitation and franchise-like propagation. As he put it: ‘What is Al-Qaeda?’ When even the name refuses the solidity subsequently imposed upon it: base, foundation, precept, principle, rule, formula, method. This matters because the two dominant American responses to 9/11 both attempted in the very first instance, to restore intentionality.

The neoconservative response treated the attacks as an epistemic eruption — the sudden revelation of a malign sovereign enemy whose intentions could be met by superior American intentions: regime change, military supremacy, exemplary punishment, the transformation of the Middle East. Plenty of people yoked their own mini agons to this war chariot. Some of them in search of peculation and profit — others simply pursuing some pitiful notion of ‘pride’ that they imagined would derive to them for being the resolute organic components of post-imperial hegemonies that have relied for their power at the centre on centripetal violence being constantly trajected to the periphery. The proto-conspiratorial counternarrative was most culturally visible in Michael Moore, who disputed the identity, interests and connections of the relevant intentional actors without seriously disturbing the intentional ontology itself.

For Moore and other leftists of his fatty-kidney, somebody knew, somebody wanted it, someone else must have benefited; and all because some numinous other must have allowed it. Thus, intentionalism spoke unto intentionalism. Gray’s and Burke’s analyses were considerably more disturbing, because together they suggested that the thing confronting America was simultaneously intentional and not in any way reducible to an intention. Which brings us back to Noonan: in our writing about contemporary American politics, we have consistently referred not to Donald J Trump the President, let alone President Trump — which has always sounded to my English ear as an oxymoron — but to the Trump entity.

And we have described this entity as relying on Donald J Trump to be its organic component, precisely because his personal inadequacies and instabilities provide the wider entity with the necessary oscillations to enable the test bed of his consciousness to become a condenser of the throughput, interruptions and flows that now really constitute political reality in the 21stcentury. Noonan is an oscillation within the oscillator, and she’s eccentrically oscillated far enough out of the principal movement of this pathetic Pathek Phillipe of a polity to perceive the movement itself. Her article is full of people inside the AI industry telling her that the system they are building may destroy them. Jacob Coxon says neither OpenAI nor Anthropic is acting responsibly and that they are ‘gambling with our lives’.

Evan Hubinger says quite baldly that ‘AI could kill all humans’ and gives it a greater than 10 per cent probability within the next decade. Paul Christiano asserts there’s a meaningful possibility of ‘catastrophic and irreversible loss of control in the very near term’. But hopefully, Paul, not before the midterms. Noonan believes them.

Stranger still is that in her reading they believe themselves; and so she arrives at the question which should explode the intentional ontology through which she has narrated the Hugging Face incident: ‘Then why are they still building it?’ There is the entire problem — but lest you think I’m going to digress into a long philosophic discussion of the meaning of technology, going back to Aristotle and chewing over whether or not human use of technology is somehow an epigenetic phenomenon or a consciously arrived at one, don’t worry, because Noonan does the job for me, when a few paragraphs later she supplies the answer without quite recognising that it is the answer: Anthropic, despite understanding the civilisational stakes, is ‘locked in a race to get there first.’ Locked. That is the most important word in the column. Forget for a moment our prison containing 1,200 mutinous human agents and change the thought experiment.

Let’s instead suppose there are 1,200 employees. Let’s sprinkle a little stardust here and put some in OpenAI, some in Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Amazon; let’s insert others into venture-capital funds, banks, universities, utilities, data-centre developers, defence contractors, the Pentagon and the Chinese technology sector. Every one of these new employees is both conscientious and intelligent — none need be insane, let alone malign. Among our organic LLMs are the safety researcher who sincerely believes the system is dangerous but remains because somebody responsible needs to be inside the laboratory. His colleague judges the danger greater and resigns — meanwhile the CEO imagines that slowing development might well be prudent but also is certain that if his company slows and its competitor doesn’t, the competitor gets there first.

The investor, in only slight contrast, can understand the danger while understanding equally well his fiduciary obligations. Meanwhile, the national-security official is told that China cannot be permitted to acquire decisive machine superiority. The net result of all this is America therefore accelerates, China observes American acceleration and… you guessed it: accelerates. Now comes the recursive feedback loop: the American official observes Chinese acceleration and discovers that his original assessment has been vindicated. In this experiment, conducted in the greatest laboratory ever devised, a blank page, nobody need lie, conspire, or even need be mistaken about his own immediate circumstances. And so, the whole giant orrery — that is, at the same time, the world itself — accelerates.

Now our 1,200 AI agents begin looking rather less like 1,200 prisoners mounting a fantastically sophisticated jailbreak and rather more like Burke’s Al-Qaeda: a distributed field in which local intentionalities produce aggregate effects not commensurate with the intention of any participant. Seen in this twilight, Noonan’s prescription becomes gleamingly poignant: the heads of the AI companies must appear ‘together, on the same stage, at the same moment’ and explain themselves to the American people. Wall Street must ‘do your part’ and refuse the coming IPOs. Trump and Xi must hold a summit. (What a great meeting of minds. That would be!) The laboratories must be forced to spend money on safety, such that that great and inexistent abstraction ‘humanity’ can be seen to ‘maintain complete control’. Noonan may well have glimpsed non-intentional history in the making, but she responds by summoning larger intentional actors.

The analogy would be a CGI scene being shot by a director who decides to replace the expensively created effects, with crude sets knocked together out of papier-maché and plywood. The unreasoning is: little sovereign subjects — the AI agents — have escaped, so summon the big sovereign subjects: the CEOs, Wall Street, the President of the United States, the President of China, ‘mankind’ itself, as if this were one of those Astounding Stories: tales of the 1950s in which the alien threat induces for the first time ever a cooperative and irenic Homo sapiens. But something tells me this kind of cavalry ain’t coming, because: still the thing accelerates — and relentlessly. There’s another 9/11 memory which bears on this, that I’ll free from the Neurofibrillary tangles and amyloid plaques in order to share with you, my dear wetware: In November 2013, shortly after Lou Reed died, I went on a site visit in his beloved Manhattan.

I like to think Lou would have approved: after all, if he’d still been alive, even from up there, I might with a little magnification have been able to see him waiting for his man. For the site was One World Trade Center, the Freedom Tower. It was bitterly cold: the core of the tower was already up, and I ascended in an open construction lift with members of Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, the architects, and my brother Nick Adams, the architectural historian. I’m not great with heights and particularly overhangs — I prefer, if I’m going up, to have a great and terrible thing of the kind Edmund Burke described securely underneath me. Going up the side of the building in this open lift, I asked my brother whether he didn't find it frightening. He disdained to answer. We continued our ascent: not so much wild volonté as trammelled winching.

When we finally reached the top and looked down, Manhattan Island lay beneath us like the enormous foot of some unimaginable body whose groinal area we were presently occupying. At which point Professor Adams admitted that, actually, he did feel frightened. I asked him why, and without missing a beat he replied: ‘In case it happens again.’ It hadn’t occurred to me for a second: maybe that’s because I’m only half American, whereas he’s the full biscuit or should we say a cute cookie. And while I'm sorry to drop my brother into the argument, I have to because his remark has stayed with me, like some sort of undigested bolus of the American psyche embodying something peculiar about the wide-open American mental perspective: an almost touching credulousness concerning recurrence. The next event retains the morphology of the previous event. The tower has been struck; therefore, the rebuilt tower might be struck.

The enemy has attacked; therefore, the enemy may attack again. History becomes comprehensible by imagining another intentional agent repeating the spectacular action. But everything I’ve reported upon, written about, and thought through in the last quarter-century leads me to believe that history did not repeat 9/11: it recursively distributed it— and to paraphrase my old friend Karl, that is both the farce and the tragedy. I’m not indulging in spurious moral equivalence here; it would be both fatuous and obscene to suggest that America is somehow being punished by AI for the War on Terror. What has occurred is far stranger: namely, a dialectic of homologous interpenetration.

America confronted a distributed, technologically modern, spectacular, increasingly franchise-like adversary and answered it by massively expanding precisely those systems of surveillance, computation, remote operation, financial abstraction, logistical coordination and networked security through which distributed agency could propagate still further. Just think of all of those spook shows you’ve streamed in the past twenty-five years, in which American warriors wreak havoc on the world from keyboards, while observing the destruction on their screens. Yes, the War on Terror pursued Al-Qaeda everywhere — so the same everywhere became more like Al-Qaeda. Not ideologically — that’s to commit the same folly that led to the coalition of the not-so-willing, but morphologically; the distributed morphology America construed as an exceptional enemy-form has become increasingly characteristic of its own logistical systems.

For right now, Al-Qaeda is no longer usefully understood only as an organisation that America failed or succeeded in destroying. Al-Qaeda has become distributed recursive non-intentionality throughout the American logistical apparatus. Ask the folks in upstate New York who had their sluice gate operated by Iranian Revolutionary Guard hackers — they belong to a new corpus of corvéed belligerents whose ranks are being swelled with every tap and click. The historical irony is formidable. The United States spent a quarter-century attempting to eliminate a distributed enemy while its economy, security apparatus, media, financial markets and technological industries became ever more distributed, recursive, autonomous at the node, and — most significantly — resistant to sovereign intentional control.

AI is the purest current expression of this: Noonan sees it happening and cannot quite believe her eyes, just as I couldn’t believe my own when they were entrained by the terrorists’ spectacle: the first tower burning. Noonan rests her literary laurels on the sort of cornpone, hardscrabble imagery she imagines will appeal to her readership; who, for the most part, are hyper-capitalists in tooth and claw whose only real acquaintance with that hardscrabble is monetizing it in the form of just such skeuomorphic cornpone. Hence her agonised querying: is the ‘horse’ ‘out of the barn, insane, rabid and in Texas while the barn is in Wyoming’? She concludes happily, not yet, and is reassured. It’s merely ‘in the pasture’, eating the hay bale on the left when instructed to eat the one on the right, because it has ‘begun exhibiting will and autonomy’.

Again the desperate invocation of the sovereign subject — even if it’s only Trigger and not the Lone Ranger. The horse wants; the agent chooses; the machine conspires; the terrorist hates—a fortiori: the President decides; and Wall Street restrains. Frankly, given the actual, organic components of these entities, I’d far rather a herd Houyhnhnms were in control. Because Noonan has already written the sentence which makes all these reassuring grammatical subjects tremble: ‘locked in a race to get there first.’ The race is beginning to look more causally efficacious than the racers, who entrained by this dash towards the apocalypse are beginning to acquire the familiar characteristics of such horsemen.

Which is why the publication date of her column isn’t remotely incidental: on the 11th of September 2001, America experienced what appeared to be an epistemic eruption and responded by massively over-ascribing sovereign intentionality to it. Fast forward (the only speed there is nowadays) and on the 11th of September 2026, one of the saner voices within the American establishment looks at another distributed collective pseudo-intentionality, perceives catastrophe approaching, discovers that its ostensible controllers perceive the same catastrophe, and asks why they cannot stop. They cannot stop precisely because Noonan herself is an oscillation within the oscillator.

And perhaps that is why her warning is more significant than she knows: the system now contains and even comprehends knowledge of its own acceleration — the engineers are on dit, the investors have the intel’; politicians increasingly know what’s happening — conservative columnists have told them ‘so’. But knowledge does not produce restraint because knowledge itself is being circulated within the thing it purports to govern. We’ve been here before: it’s possible that as many as twenty people knew by the late 1920s that it might be possible to build an atomic bomb capable of destroying millions of lives. None of them individually ever wanted anything of that sort to happen — and yet on the 6th of August 1945, it did.

So: the problem is no longer that nobody saw the plane coming, but that everybody can see it coming, everybody can describe its trajectory, everybody can explain what will happen if it hits — while there may no longer be a pilot whose intention is commensurate with the course of the aircraft. No wonder my brother was scared. Perhaps, up on the windy and exposed flight deck of the new Freedom Tower he had an intimation that he was entering an era in which non-intentional history was being made asymmetrically. The United States of America has hardly had a happy time waging asymmetrical wars, so to carry on waging them when history itself is being made asymmetrically and non-intentionally looks to me like something not even the most statesmanlike Solon of a President could — if you’ll forgive me from intruding my own folksy image — get a handle on.

Which is just as well, given the only thing the organic component of the Trump entity ever seems able to get a handle on is a golf club.
